nameStory: The word 'potato' comes from the Spanish 'patata,' which was borrowed from the Taíno word 'batata' - though that originally referred to sweet potatoes! When Spanish explorers brought these starchy tubers back from South America in the 1500s, the names got mixed up, and 'potato' stuck for what we now call the regular potato.
description: The potato plant is a bushy, leafy annual that grows 2-3 feet tall with compound leaves and small white or purple star-shaped flowers. Most people only see the underground tubers we eat, but the above-ground plant has a distinctive appearance with its dark green, somewhat fuzzy foliage. The plant produces small, round green fruits that look like tiny tomatoes - which makes sense since they're close relatives!

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white or light purple star-shaped flowers with five pointed petals and bright yellow centers, growing in loose clusters. The flowers have a delicate, slightly sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-9 oval leaflets of varying sizes, arranged alternately on stems. The leaves feel slightly rough and fuzzy to the touch, with a distinctive 'green' smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, round green berries about the size of cherry tomatoes that develop after flowering. These fruits are toxic and should never be eaten - they contain dangerous levels of solanine.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy, upright plant growing 2-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems. The stems are often tinged with purple and feel somewhat succulent when squeezed gently.

idTips.label: Underground Tubers
idTips.description: The familiar brown-skinned potato tubers grow on underground stems called stolons. Fresh-dug tubers have thin, papery skin that rubs off easily and smell earthy and starchy.

habitat: In New England, you'll find potato plants in cultivated fields, gardens, and occasionally as volunteers in compost piles or disturbed soil where potatoes were previously grown. They prefer well-drained, loose soil and full sun. Escaped plants sometimes appear along field edges or in farmyard areas.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are planted in late spring after frost danger passes, and young plants emerge as bushy green shoots. Early growth shows the characteristic compound leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and bloom with their distinctive white or purple star flowers from mid to late summer. This is when the plant is most easily identified by its flowers and full foliage.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to yellow and die back as tubers mature underground. The small green fruits become more noticeable as the foliage starts to decline.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts are completely dead and gone. Only dormant tubers remain underground, occasionally sprouting if left in the ground over winter.

funFact: Potato plants are actually toxic above ground - the leaves, stems, and those little green fruits contain solanine, the same poison found in deadly nightshade, which can cause serious illness or even death if eaten in large quantities!
confusionNotes: The small green fruits are often mistaken for cherry tomatoes by children, but these are extremely toxic. Remember: if you see small round green fruits on a potato-like plant, never eat them - only the underground tubers are safe to consume.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that the 'eyes' on potatoes are actually buds on underground stems, not roots - potatoes are technically modified stems called tubers, not root vegetables like carrots or radishes.
compareHints: Unlike its nightshade relatives, potato has compound leaves rather than simple ones, and produces edible underground tubers. The flowers are very similar to tomato flowers but typically smaller and often purple-tinged. Unlike the toxic berries of other nightshades, potato's edible parts are underground - though its above-ground berries are just as poisonous as those of bittersweet nightshade.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other nightshades in New England, bittersweet nightshade is the only one that grows as a climbing vine with purple flowers.
Among New England's nightshades, Carolina horsenettle is the only one covered in sharp prickles, making it instantly recognizable.
Unlike bittersweet nightshade which has purple flowers and grows as a climbing vine, eastern black nightshade has white flowers and grows as a low bushy annual.
Among its nightshade relatives in New England, tomato is easily distinguished by its large, edible red fruit and cultivation in gardens.
Among New England nightshades, buffalo-bur is unmistakable due to its extreme spininess - no other Solanum species is nearly as heavily armed with spines.
Black nightshade differs from its cousin bittersweet nightshade by being much smaller and having white flowers instead of purple ones with swept-back petals.
Hairy nightshade differs from eastern black nightshade by its distinctly hairy stems and leaves (black nightshade is mostly smooth).

Green nightshade stands apart from its New England nightshade relatives primarily by its persistently green, glossy berries - eastern black nightshade and black nightshade both produce dark purple-black berries when ripe, while bittersweet nightshade produces bright red berries.
Unlike its wild nightshade relatives that grow as weeds in New England, cultivated eggplant is much larger in all aspects - bigger leaves, bigger flowers, and dramatically bigger fruits.

Garden huckleberry differs from other nightshades in New England by its drooping clusters of dark berries and relatively benign nature – unlike bittersweet nightshade with its bright red berries, or the more weedy black nightshade species.
Unlike other nightshades in New England, red buffalo-bur is the most heavily armed with prickles covering every surface.
